Delhi HC seeks response from Centre, FSSAI on plea seeking ban on sale of analogue products as paneer
A bench of acting chief justice Nitin Sambre and justice Sanjay Sharma sought the Centre, FSSAI and Delhi government’s response in six weeks.
Updated on: Oct 14, 2026, 13:46:27 IST
By
Shruti Kakkar

The Delhi high court on Wednesday issued notice on a petition seeking to restrain the manufacture and sale of analogue products allegedly being passed off as paneer in the national capital.
Unlike traditional paneer, analogue paneer is made from vegetable oils, starches, plant proteins, emulsifiers, and food additives rather than milk (Photos: shutterstock (for representational purpose only))
A bench of acting chief justice Nitin Sambre and justice Sanjay Sharma sought the Centre, FSSAI and Delhi government’s response in a petition filed by one law student, Ridhima Singh, and advocate AP Siddharth in six weeks.
Analogue paneer is a product made to look, feel and function like paneer, but in which some or all milk constituents are replaced with ingredients not derived from milk.
Last month, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) proposed restrictions on the manufacture and sale of paneer made with non-milk constituents. The draft amendment, published on September 24, seeks to add “paneer made of constituents not derived from milk” to the list of substances whose sale is prohibited.
Products already licensed or registered as “Analogue in Dairy Context” would have to drop the word “paneer” from their name, labelling and marketing.
Meanwhile, in their plea before the high court, the two petitioners asserted that Food Safety Authorities in different states, such as Maharashtra, Gujarat, Punjab and Chhattisgarh, have already taken preventive and enforcement measures in relation to analogue/non dairy paneer under the FSSAI Act and thus, such an action also needs to be taken in Delhi.
“That Delhi cannot be treated as being removed from the above regulatory concern. The NCT of Delhi is one of the largest markets for milk products, paneer and paneer-based food preparations and has an enormous network of restaurants, hotels, caterers, cloud kitchens, wholesalers, retailers and food-delivery establishments,” the petition said.
Singh’s petition also sought an order by the Commissioner of Food Safety to prohibit such manufacture. It said that paneer is one of the most widely consumed sources of protein across vast sections, and that the right of consumers to receive a food article that genuinely conforms to the nature, substance, and quality demanded has a nexus with the fundamental right to health enshrined under Article 21.
Delhi government standing counsel Sameer Vashisth submitted that the government was taking action against the sale of analogue paneer and acted as soon as such instances came to its notice.

The Delhi High Court on Wednesday (October 14, 2026) sought the stand of the FSSAI, the Centre and the city government on a PIL raising concerns over the sale of dairy analogue/non-dairy products as ‘paneer’ to unsuspecting consumers.
What is analogue paneer, and why is FSSAI cracking down on it? | Explained
The petitioners contended that while paneer is a standardised dairy product under the food safety regime, a non-dairy, analogue product contains non-milk ingredients and lacks the same nutritional value.
A Bench of acting Chief Justice Nitin W. Sambre and Justice Sanjay Singh issued notices to the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), the Centre and the Delhi government on the petition filed by Ridhima Singh and Avlokiteshwar Padmapani Sidharth, and asked them to file their replies within six weeks.
What is ‘analogue’ paneer, which the Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra and Gujarat governments have banned?
The petitioners contended that a person consuming a paneer-based product in a hotel or a restaurant has no means to know whether the dish is prepared using actual paneer or a dairy analogue.
They sought urgent directions from the court in view of the festive season, asserting that the authorities should undertake sampling and testing of paneer and products represented as paneer in the market.
“They are doing it, they have placed the statistics (before us) to that effect,” the bench responded.
Karnataka bans sale of analogue paneer under the name ‘paneer’ for one year
The plea said that Gujarat, Punjab, Chhattisgarh and Maharashtra have already taken steps against non-dairy paneer, and sought directions to the authorities to prevent the manufacture, supply, sale or service of dairy analogue paneer in the capital.
It also prayed for directions to the authorities to ensure that hotels, restaurants, caterers, eateries, cloud kitchens and e-commerce food businesses provide clear disclosure on the use of analogue/non-dairy substitutes in their food.
Maharashtra govt. bans analogue paneer for one year, cites food safety norm violations
“A consumer who knowingly purchases a product correctly disclosed as an analogue or non-dairy substitute makes an informed choice. However, a consumer who purchases or orders ‘paneer’ is entitled to receive a product which answers the statutory description of paneer and ought not to be unknowingly supplied a product in which essential milk constituents have been substituted by vegetable fat, vegetable oil or other non-milk constituents,” the petition said.

File Photo: Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust decides to conduct 100 percent verification of all staff working at the Ram temple in Ayodhya.
The Ram temple in Ayodhya has received the highest rating under the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India’s (FSSAI) ‘Eat Right Place of Worship’ initiative, recognising its efforts to maintain food safety and hygiene standards while preparing and distributing prasad.
The Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra scored 103 out of 114 points in the assessment, earning the ‘Ati Vishisht’ rating under the BHOG (Blissful Hygienic Offering to God) programme. Five other places of worship in Ayodhya, including Hanumangarhi, Kanak Bhawan, a Jain temple and Devkali temple, also received BHOG certification.
The initiative aims to ensure that food offerings served to devotees are prepared, stored and distributed safely, particularly at places of worship that see large numbers of visitors.
Ram temple receives highest rating for food safety
The certification was presented during a programme in Ayodhya attended by FSSAI chief executive officer Rajit Punhani and officials from the Uttar Pradesh Food Safety and Drug Administration (UPFSDA).
Speaking at the event, Punhani highlighted the importance of maintaining food safety at religious institutions.
“Prasad is not merely food; it is a symbol of faith and dignity. Ensuring that devotees receive safe and quality prasad is a collective responsibility,” he was quoted as saying by Hindustan Times.
The certification will remain valid for two years. During this period, state and central authorities will conduct inspections and audits to check whether the prescribed standards are being followed. The temple trust will also carry out internal reviews every fortnight using a checklist to monitor compliance.
Trust general secretary Govind Dev Giri said maintaining the purity of prasad was especially important because of its religious and cultural significance.
“Cleanliness is akin to divinity,” he said, stressing the need to maintain hygiene during both the preparation and distribution of prasad. He described the certification as recognition of the temple’s efforts to uphold food safety standards.
How does the BHOG certification work?
The BHOG programme is part of FSSAI’s wider ‘Eat Right’ initiative, which promotes safe and nutritious food across different settings.
According to Rekha Chauhan, UPFSDA special secretary and additional commissioner, the certification process involves auditing the kitchens, storage facilities and food-serving areas of religious institutions against prescribed food safety standards, as reported by Hindustan Times.
The process has five stages. It begins with verification of a valid FSSAI licence or registration, followed by an inspection conducted by an authorised auditor. Designated supervisors also undergo food safety training under the Food Safety Training and Certification (FoSTaC) programme.
The institution is then assessed against a checklist covering 47 parameters, with a maximum possible score of 114. FSSAI reviews the assessment and approves the recommendation before issuing the certificate.
What do the different FSSAI ratings mean?
The ‘Ati Vishisht’ rating is the highest category under the scheme. Religious institutions scoring between 100 and 114 points qualify for it.
Those scoring between 91 and 99 receive the ‘Santoshjanak’ (satisfactory) rating. Institutions scoring between 77 and 90 are required to undergo another audit after making improvements, while those scoring below 77 must reapply.
With 103 points, the Ram temple falls in the highest category.
The certification programme also includes training for food handlers, helping religious institutions strengthen hygiene practices and improve the way offerings are prepared and served to devotees.
FSSAI officials, including executive directors Umashankar Dhyani and Dr Amit Sharma, regional director Devesh Kumar Mahla and manager Ananya Pandey, attended the programme along with representatives of the temple trust.

View Market Dashboard What happens to 'energy drinks' after Campa, PepsiCo get interim court relief against FSSAI label ban? | Explained As Reliance’s Campa, PepsiCo and Monster receive interim relief from the Delhi High Court against an FSSAI order prohibiting them from marketing high-caffeine beverages as “energy drinks”, the question remains: What happens to the existing stock? Swati Gandhi Published 7 Oct 2026, 02:46 PM IST Prefer Livemint on Google PepsiCo, Campa, Monster vs FSSAI: All you need to know ( X/Instagram ) AI Quick Read The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India’s ( FSSAI ) action against potentially misleading claims suffered a temporary setback on Tuesday after the Delhi High Court granted interim relief to Reliance Consumer Products in its dispute with the regulator over the use of the term “energy drink” on high-caffeine Campa beverages. With PepsiCo, Reliance’s Campa and Monster now receiving interim relief, questions remain about what happens to products already in stores, as well as stocks that were withdrawn or seized following FSSAI’s direction. Can they continue to be sold or automatically return to shelves? Also Read | Reliance sues FSSAI for preventing it from marketing Campa-brand products What did the Delhi High Court say? On Tuesday, Reliance Consumer Products moved the Delhi High Court, seeking relief from the FSSAI order prohibiting the company from marketing products under its Campa brand as “energy drinks”. The court questioned the food safety regulator over its directive and asked why the company had not been issued a notice before the order was passed. Further, the court told FSSAI that it was “never too late” to correct its mistake. The court clarified that the temporary relief applies only to products already manufactured and does not permit the companies to produce new batches carrying the “energy drink” label. The stay will continue until the next hearing on 5 November. What did the companies say? According to its petition, Reliance argued that state authorities had seized Campa stock and directed e-commerce platforms to delist the products. Both Reliance and PepsiCo informed the court that they would suffer huge losses due to FSSAI’s order. Also Read | FSSAI orders Pepsi, Red Bull, Monster to drop ‘energy drink’ label Reliance Consumer Products told the Delhi High Court that its existing stock included 168 million cans and 120 million plastic bottles marked as “energy drink”. The company also had packaging carrying the same description ready for a further 400 million cans and 360 million bottles. PepsiCo said that 492 million bottles and 26 million cans bearing the disputed label were in circulation as of 31 July. What happens to the existing stock? In the present case, the Delhi High Court has allowed the companies to sell their existing stock carrying the disputed label. However, they cannot manufacture new batches bearing the description while the interim arrangement remains in force. Ashwin Bhadri, founder and CEO of Equinox Labs, explains that food packaging is planned months in advance, and by the time a dispute reaches the courts, products may already be sitting in warehouses, with distributors or on retail shelves. Businesses must then determine whether the stock should be held, recalled, reworked, relabelled or allowed to remain in circulation, with substantial costs potentially passing through the supply chain. FSSAI order: What we know The dispute between the beverage brands and the food safety regulator stemmed from a 30 June order in which FSSAI directed companies selling high-caffeine beverages to stop using “energy drinks” and related terms. Further, it gave the companies three months to revise their product labels and packaging accordingly. The disagreement centres on whether drinks containing high levels of caffeine may be promoted and labelled as “energy drinks”. While the regulator has moved to limit the use of the term, manufacturers contend that altering their established labels could result in substantial financial losses. You pick up an apple, peel off the little sticker, give it a good wash and take a bite. Seems perfectly fine, right?
Well, there’s one extra step India’s food safety regulator wants you to follow.
The
Food Safety and Standards Authority of India
(FSSAI) has advised consumers not to simply remove stickers from fruits and vegetables and wash the produce. Instead, it says the skin or the portion where the sticker was placed should be peeled or cut away before eating.
The reason? The adhesive used to stick those tiny labels to the produce can leave residue behind.
So, what should you actually do?
It's pretty simple.
If there's a sticker on your apple, orange, avocado or any other fruit, remove it first.
Then peel the skin or cut away the small patch where the sticker was attached.
You don't need to throw away the fruit. And there's no need to panic if you've already eaten a stickered fruit after simply washing it.
The advice is essentially about taking an extra precaution and avoiding direct consumption of any residue that may be left behind.
Why are fruits covered in stickers anyway?
Those little labels are something most of us barely notice, especially when doing our weekly grocery shopping.
But they're there for a reason. Fruit stickers can carry codes used by retailers to identify the produce and its price. Depending on the product and retailer, they may also provide other information about the fruit.
What they aren't, however, is edible packaging.
So even if the sticker comes off easily, it's better not to assume that the surface underneath is completely free of adhesive.
Is washing the fruit not enough?
Washing your fruits and vegetables is still important. But in the case of produce that has had a sticker stuck directly onto its skin, FSSAI's advice is to go one step further.
Remove the sticker and then peel or cut away the area where it was stuck.
For something like an apple, that's easy enough. If you're eating the fruit without peeling it, simply cutting off that small patch is another option.
Why the sticker maybe harmful?
Don't panic.
If you've ever discovered halfway through eating an apple that the tiny sticker has somehow vanished, you're certainly not alone
Do you need to throw the fruit away?
No.
A sticker doesn't mean the entire fruit is unsafe. Once you've removed the label, simply peel or cut off the area where it was attached.
And yes, you should still wash the fruit properly before eating it and that's because the glue in the sticker maybe harmful for your health.
The next time you're about to bite into that supermarket apple, take a second look at the sticker. Peel it off, remove the small stickered patch and then eat the fruit.
It's a tiny extra step. But when it comes to something you eat, it doesn't hurt to be a little careful.

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) had issued a directive to food safety authorities across all states and union territories to step up surveillance and enforcement actions against unsafe food products in light of the upcoming festive season.
The festive season typically brings a spike in demand for multiple food items such as milk and milk products, sweets, snacks and savouries including Namkeen, papad/fryums, edible oil, beverages, ghee, etc. (PTI/ Representational)
The festive season typically brings a spike in demand for multiple food items such as dairy products, sweets, snacks and savouries including Namkeen, papad/fryums, edible oil, beverages, ghee, etc.
FSSAI calls for heightened surveillance, strict action
As per the directive, heightened inspection and enforcement actions are meant to prevent the circulation of “adulterated, counterfeited and unsafe food products”. Beyond the food items mentioned, the FSSAI also asks regional agencies to expand the list of targeted commodities as per local eating and consumption patterns.
In order to address this public health concern, all enforcement officials (Designated Officers/ Food Safety Officers/ Central Food Safety Officers), under the directives of their respective commissioners, will be deployed to conduct inspection and sampling in their respective regions during the festive period. As per judgement, food hot spots and other sensitive locations are to come under special focus in this matter.
In addition, the order calls for the strategic deployment of Food Safety on Wheels (FSWs), a functional mobile laboratory for food testing, in prominent market areas. Based on intel received, the initiative is meant to push for on-spot-testing of food safety norms, strengthening hygiene vigilance and boosting consumer confidence during a period of flooded demand in the market.
All relevant data in lieu with inspection, sampling, and outcome must mandatorily be uploaded or recorded on FoSCoS/FoSCoRIS on a real-time basis, the notice further states.

in Govindpura, Manimajra last Thursday after the health department found the vendor running the business in unhygienic conditions, without registering with the FSSAI.
The official of the food safety administration revealed that the kitchen of the vendor concerned was found dirty, with food not stored properly and kept in open, walls not being properly painted, workers in shabby clothes, dirty utensils, and unhygienic washing area.

The Delhi high court has temporarily halted the FSSAI's directive concerning the Campa Energy Drink
NEW DELHI: The
Delhi high court
on Tuesday stayed a
Food Safety and Standards Authority of India
(
FSSAI
) order directing Reliance Consumer Products Ltd (RCPL) to remove the "Energy Drink" descriptor from its Campa Energy Drink - Gold Boost, providing interim relief to the company in its challenge against the regulator's action.
Justice Amit Mahajan also stayed the consequential communication issued by the FSSAI on July 17, 2026, and all further steps taken pursuant to the June 30 order and the subsequent communication.
The June 30 order had directed RCPL to remove the descriptor "Energy Drink" from its Campa Energy Drink - Gold Boost.
The July 17 communication had asked the Commissioners of Food Safety of all States and Union Territories to take steps to enforce the June 30 direction against RCPL.
The company challenged both the original FSSAI order and the subsequent communication before the Delhi high court.
HC cites lack of show-cause notice before FSSAI action
The court granted interim protection to RCPL after noting that the FSSAI directions had been issued without first serving the company with a show-cause notice or giving it an opportunity to present its case.
The plea argued that the action was contrary to the principles of natural justice, under which a person or entity likely to be affected by an administrative decision should be given a fair opportunity of hearing.
The high court's order means that, during the pendency of the proceedings, the June 30 direction requiring RCPL to drop the "Energy Drink" descriptor from Campa Energy Drink - Gold Boost will remain stayed, along with the consequential enforcement communication and steps taken under it.
FSSAI order relates to ‘Energy Drink’ descriptor
The dispute concerns the use of the term "Energy Drink" for beverages containing caffeine.
FSSAI had issued its June 30 direction to manufacturers concerning the description used for certain high-caffeine beverages.
RCPL subsequently approached the high court challenging the action taken against its Campa product.
During the hearing, the court also questioned the regulator about the procedure followed before issuing the direction. The court observed that it was "never too late" for the authority to correct the issue, according to the submissions recorded during the proceedings.
Other beverage firms also challenge FSSAI direction
The matter assumes significance as similar challenges have also been raised before the Delhi high court by other beverage companies following the FSSAI's directions concerning the use of the "Energy Drink" descriptor.
RCPL was represented by Senior Advocate Sandeep Sethi, instructed by Karanjawala & Co. The legal team was led by Senior Partner Ruby Singh Ahuja and comprised Advocates Ravneet Kaur Malik, Piyush Sharma, Abhyuday Mishra and VAswal.

Experts advocate for simpler food labels
Saloni, a nutritionist and founder of Femly, told
LiveMint

Elaborating, she said, "When you're standing in a supermarket, you shouldn't need to be a nutritionist to figure out what you're buying. Consumers should be able to look at a packet and quickly understand the basics: what are the main ingredients, how much sugar, sodium and saturated fat does it contain."

When asked whether Indians should be worried about complex terms on the backs of products, the two experts explained that they shouldn't be worried, but they must be informed. "Natural" or "herbal" does not automatically mean chemical-free or safer than synthetic ingredients.
Dose matters:
The risk of an additive depends on how much is consumed, so consumers should consider portion size and overall nutrition.
Sugar can hide behind different names:
Ingredients such as maltodextrin, dextrose, rice syrup and invert sugar can make it harder to identify total sugar intake.

FSSAI: M/s Everest Food Products Private Limited has been directed to immediately recall "Pre-packed Cumin Powder" after tests declared the sample "UNSAFE".
One batch of a popular cumin powder has now been pulled into a food-safety investigation after a laboratory sample was declared “UNSAFE”. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has ordered an immediate recall of the implicated batch of Everest pre-packed cumin powder after testing found two pesticide residues above the prescribed maximum limits.
The recall raises a more everyday question for consumers: what should genuine cumin look like, and can adulteration be spotted at home?
2
/
5
Why FSSAI recalled the cumin powder
According to FSSAI, a regulatory sample of pre-packed cumin powder was collected from the premises of Riverside Resorts & Holiday Homes Pvt Ltd in Goa.
The Food Analyst detected residues of Azoxystrobin and Thiamethoxam at levels exceeding the prescribed maximum limits. The sample was consequently declared “UNSAFE” under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
The batch number identified in the recall is E080668761. FSSAI also directed the company to maintain records of the recalled product, submit the required recall information and take corrective measures to prevent a recurrence.
3
/
5
Cumin powder is easier to adulterate
There is another reason consumers often find it difficult to judge powdered spices.
FSSAI has pointed out that spices sold in ground form can be easier to adulterate because consumers cannot easily see what went into the powder. Its food-safety material lists several substances that may be mixed into ground spices, including cheaper materials such as flour, starch, sawdust and chalk powder.
For cumin specifically, FSSAI has identified coloured grass seeds and fennel seeds among possible adulterants.
That is where whole cumin seeds offer one simple advantage: you can actually look at them.
4
/
5
How to check cumin seeds at home
FSSAI's consumer-awareness material includes simple household tests for common adulterants.
For cumin seeds, one test involves rubbing the seeds between your palms. If the palms turn black, FSSAI says it indicates possible adulteration with grass seeds coloured with charcoal dust.
Another FSSAI DART test is specifically designed to detect fennel seeds mixed with cumin. The recommended method is visual: place a small quantity of cumin seeds on a glass plate and examine them closely. Fennel seeds can be separated by careful observation.
For powdered spices, FSSAI also provides rapid household tests through its Detect Adulteration with Rapid Test (DART) programme. The regulator says its DART booklet contains more than 50 tests covering different food products and common adulterants.
But a home test is only a quick screening method. It cannot establish whether a packaged product contains pesticide residues or whether a particular chemical is above its legally permitted limit. Such findings require laboratory testing.
5
/
5
What consumers should check now
The immediate point for anyone who has the recalled product at home is simple: check the batch number before using it. If it is E080668761, it is the batch covered by the FSSAI recall.
FSSAI maintains a public food-recall system so consumers can check information about unsafe or non-compliant food products withdrawn from the market.
And the larger lesson goes beyond one packet of cumin. A spice can look, smell and taste normal and still require laboratory testing to establish whether it meets food-safety standards. For consumers, buying properly labelled products, checking recall information and knowing the basic visual signs of adulteration can add one more layer of protection in the kitchen.

In a separate action, the regulator also suspended the licence of Creative Bakers and Confectioners Pvt Ltd – which operates the retail chain The Sugarr & Spice across several outlets in Eastern India – with immediate effect over serious hygiene, sanitation and food safety violations.
The FSSAI has, over the past six months, stepped up enforcement actions, and relays them to the food business operators and the public through its official handles on social media platforms.

‘Pesticide residues exceeding maximum limits’: FSSAI on Everest cumin powder recall

The Food Analyst's report of this sample found the product to have pesticide residues of Azoxystrobin and Thiamethoxam at levels exceeding the prescribed maximum limit, it said.

Following this, the entire batch of the product was directed to be recalled immediately from the market, and Everest was ordered to “maintain complete records of the recalled product and submit the prescribed recall information and status reports within the stipulated timelines.”

The regulator said it found perishable raw materials being stored “openly”, adding that rusted and inadequately cleaned containers were being used for raw and semi-finished products. “Significant pest infestation and inadequate pest-control measures were observed, including ineffective fly control, absence of proper rodent control and openings/windows without insect-proof mesh,” FSSAI added.
It said that waste, old stock, rejected lots and scrap were found to be accumulated in the food handling areas of the confectioner's premises, while rusting equipment, flaking paint, dampness and broken floor tiles were also observed. “Required food safety records and systems, including water and finished-product testing, time-temperature monitoring, calibration, preventive maintenance, mock recall, consumer complaints, straining and audit records, were not properly maintained,” the regulator added. NEW DELHI: Sonal Machchhar, wife of Indian pilot Captain Smit Machchhar, recalled the horrifying moment she learnt about the mid-air attack on her husband aboard a flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv, saying she was "very devastated" and did not have the immediate "mental capacity" to comprehend the crisis.
In a conversation with a news channel, Sonal described being overcome with shock after hearing the news, news agency ANI reported.
"I was very devastated. And I didn’t have the mental capacity (to know) how I should react," she said.
She said the presence of friends and family, along with updates from Indian authorities, offered her reassurance during the ordeal.

"But as I had my friends and family around me, I was reassured that everything is okay.
And very soon, I started getting news that he is stable," she said.
Sonal met her husband on Thursday at a hospital in Abu Dhabi, which helped ease her concerns about his condition, ANI reported.
Reflecting on the meeting, she said, "I met him on Thursday, and that gives me reassurance that he is in the right hands, very good care, under the good care of UAE doctors, military doctors."
Sonal said her immediate focus was on helping her husband recover.
"And I’m just hoping that he comes back home soon, and I’m going to do whatever it takes for his recovery," she said.
Asked about reports that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu wanted to speak with Captain Machchhar, Sonal said the conversation should take place directly between them once her husband has recovered sufficiently, ANI reported.
"I will not be able to talk to Mr Netanyahu. I think Smit is the right person; he should answer to Mr Netanyahu," she said, adding that "he will definitely talk to him once he is in the right frame of mind."
Earlier on Friday, Captain Machchhar spoke to Prime Minister Narendra Modi over the phone and recalled the moments after he collapsed on the floor following the attack.
He said his 17 years of flying experience helped him realise that the aircraft was going down.
The captain said that while he was consciously telling himself that he was acting for his own survival, he knew deep down that he could not allow the passengers to die.
The Prime Minister praised Machchhar's courage, patience and presence of mind and said his actions had made the country proud, ANI reported.
The September 30 security crisis involved a flydubai flight operating from Dubai to Tel Aviv, where the Omani co-pilot allegedly stabbed the commander in an apparent terror-driven attempt to bring down the plane.
The confrontation triggered a steep descent, with the aircraft dropping approximately 16,000 feet within two minutes before a hijacking distress signal was transmitted.
Despite sustaining severe injuries, Captain Machchhar resisted the assailant.
Flight crew members and passengers then breached the flight deck and restrained the attacker, allowing the crew to regain control of the aircraft.
The plane subsequently made an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, where all 180 occupants disembarked safely, ANI reported.
The captain managed to repel the co-pilot sufficiently to unlatch the cockpit entry, while two non-duty aviators on board assumed control of the aircraft for its emergency landing in Tabuk.
The identity of the co-pilot has not been publicly disclosed.
The co-pilot was transferred to the UAE after his arrest.
Israeli investigative personnel have also been sent to the UAE to join the locally led inquiry and help determine whether outside parties orchestrated the attack.

The Madras High Court has declined to withdraw its interim direction requiring packaged drinking water, sugar and salt to carry declarations about the possible presence of microplastics, holding that consumers must be informed even as scientific research into the particles’ health effects continues.
A Division Bench of Justices N Sathish Kumar and D Bharatha Chakravarthy dismissed the review petition filed by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) and applications seeking recall of the February 6, 2026, order by industry associations. The 38-page order was pronounced on September 28, seen by

The Bench held that disclosing the possible presence of microplastics was a basic consumer-information measure and did not amount to declaring the products unsafe.
What did the February order require?
The High Court’s February 6 interim order followed findings recorded in an FSSAI report concerning commercially available packaged drinking water, sugar and salt.

Microplastics were detected in bottled drinking water collected from Rajasthan, Himachal Pradesh, Chandigarh, Haryana, Karnataka and Maharashtra. The report also indicated higher levels of microplastics in sugar and salt packed in plastic or polythene packaging.
The FSSAI had told the Court that further research was necessary to establish the precise health effects of microplastics, including the quantities that the human body could tolerate.
The Court directed that plastic or PET bottles containing drinking water carry the declaration “This water may contain Micro/Nano Plastics”. The warning was to appear in bold red letters, in a font size of at least 10.
Packaged sugar and salt were similarly required to carry the statement “This Sugar/Salt may contain Micro/Nano Plastics”.
The FSSAI was directed to notify the relevant manufacturers within four weeks of receiving the order uploaded on the court website and ensure compliance with the labelling requirements.
Why did FSSAI and industry associations seek a recall?
The FSSAI, the PET Packaging Association for Clean Environment (PACE) and the Federation of All India Packaged Drinking Water Manufacturers Associations sought reconsideration of the interim direction.
Their principal argument was that mandatory warnings were premature and disproportionate because scientific research had not conclusively established the harmful effects of microplastics at the levels detected in food and drinking water.
The FSSAI argued that the regulator needed to complete further studies before deciding whether additional labelling was warranted. It also maintained that regulatory measures should be evidence-based and proportionate, taking into account possible consumer panic, disruption to supply chains and the interests of food businesses.
Another concern was that the particles found in packaged water might have originated from the water source or environmental contamination, rather than exclusively from PET bottles.
PACE relied on existing Bureau of Indian Standards requirements governing packaging materials, including migration tests and prescribed limits. It also cited the World Health Organization’s report on microplastics in drinking water, arguing that the available evidence did not establish a human health concern.
The manufacturers’ associations further contended that the products complied with existing packaging and labelling regulations, which did not specifically require disclosures about microplastics. They argued that the Court should allow the FSSAI to discharge its statutory responsibilities and frame appropriate regulations.
Why did the Court reject these arguments?
The Bench said the interim order did not declare bottled water, sugar or salt to be unsafe. It required only disclosure of the possible presence of microplastics while further scientific studies continued.
